newsitem.title: USA: CBOT, LIFFE reiterate linkage to start on time.
newsitem.headline: CBOT, LIFFE reiterate linkage to start on time.

text.p: Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) chairman Patrick Arbor and London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) chairman Jack Wigglesworth reiterated their resolve to start their open-outcry linkage on time on May 9.

Last week CBOT directors voted to ask LIFFE to make some changes to their linkup agreement that could sap business away from trade in CBOT products on LIFFE floor, raising concerns about a possible delay.

"We think the proposal will have very little impact on the start of the link-up," Arbor said as he handed Wigglesworth a copy of the CBOT's proposal letter on Friday. The two chairmen were interviewed together by Reuters in Tucson, Arizona, while attending a conference on risk management.
"The important thing is to get the link off the ground on May 9 with whatever relatively minor modification accommodated between now and then," Wigglesworth added.

Under the new CBOT proposal, U.S. T-bond trading on CBOT's Project A electronic system would go on longer than in the original agreement, overlapping with LIFFE's pit session. LIFFE's APT after-hours electronic trading for European government bond derivatives would also be longer, overlapping with the CBOT pit session.
Arbor said European customers would probably prefer using LIFFE, and the Project A trading would not necessarily drain volume from the floor.
"Some may prefer to trade electronically, some may prefer to use open outcry," he said.
"We think that it would open up arbitrage opportunity between the two markets," he added.

Wigglesworth said the CBOT-LIFFE linkage was a strategic initiative, which for LIFFE meant a stronger distribution platform for its European contracts, most notably the German government bond futures, ahead of the planned European Monetary Union. LIFFE is in fierce competition with other European exchanges over future business in the euro, the common currency to be created under EMU.
"The minor modifications...to the original agreement are very much secondary to that big cause," he said.

Wigglesworth said both exchanges were primarily open-outcry markets and they were firmly committed to the open-outcry system, even though they had seen significant growth in their electronic trading systems in recent years.
He pointed out that the exchanges have been investing millions of dollars on floor expansion.

The CBOT's new T-bond floor is due to open on February 18. Arbor said the $182 million project aimed to provide better "sight-lines" into the pit for brokers taking customer orders and more space for booths and a larger pit to accommodate bigger business. CBOT is also investing $10-20 million to revamp the agricultural products floor.
LIFFE is also investing some 30 million sterling for expansion, Wigglesworth said.
Arbor said LIFFE and the Chicago Mercantile Exchange saw an "explosion" after their previous floor expansions and predicted a similarily dramatic volume increase at CBOT.
